hints: Think about what hot, concentrated, acidified manganate(VII) does to a C=C bond compared with cold, dilute conditions, it cleaves the double bond completely.
walkthrough:
Spot the conditions for cleavage**
You have $\text{HO}_{2}\text{CCH=CHCO}_{2}\text{H}$ plus hot, concentrated, acidified $\text{MnO}_{4}^{-}$. Cold dilute would just add two OH groups across the double bond, but hot concentrated is much more vigorous. It breaks the $\text{C=C}$ bond entirely and oxidises each alkene carbon as far as it can go.

Follow each carbon to its highest oxidation product**
Each $\text{C}$ of the $\text{C=C}$ is already attached to a $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ group. Once the $\text{C=C}$ is cleaved, those fragments are oxidised to $\text{CO}_{2}$. Any $\text{C-H}$ fragments would also give $\text{CO}_{2}$ plus $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Here all four carbons end up as $\text{CO}_{2}$, with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ formed from the hydrogens.

hints: Remember addition polymerisation simply opens the $\text{C=C}$ to a $\text{C-C}$ single bond, the two $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ groups stay unchanged on adjacent carbons.
walkthrough:
Open the double bond**
Picture the monomer $\text{HO}_{2}\text{C-CH=CH-CO}_{2}\text{H}$. In addition polymerisation nothing is lost. The pi bond breaks and each alkene carbon gains one new $\text{C-C}$ bond to the next monomer. So $\text{CH=CH}$ becomes $\text{CH-CH}$ in the chain.

Draw one repeat unit correctly**
Draw a $\text{-C-C-}$ backbone with two continuation bonds, one on each carbon extending out of the unit. Put $\text{H}$ and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ on the top carbon and $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$ and $\text{H}$ on the bottom carbon, or any equivalent arrangement. The key is two carbons, each bearing one $\text{H}$ and one $\text{CO}_{2}\text{H}$.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-[CH(CO}_{2}\text{H)-CH(CO}_{2}\text{H)]-}$ with continuation bonds through the backbone carbons.

hints: Recall a polyester forms by $\text{COOH + OH}$ giving $\text{COO}$ ester plus water, so identify which O comes from the diol and which $\text{C=O}$ comes from fumaric acid.
Keep the $\text{C=C}$ from fumaric acid intact in the middle of the repeat unit and add continuation bonds at both ends of the combined diol plus diacid unit.
walkthrough:
Build the ester links**
Take $\text{HO-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-OH}$ and $\text{HOOC-CH=CH-COOH}$. Each $\text{COOH}$ reacts with one $\text{OH}$ to give $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ plus $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. So the diol contributes $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-}$ and the diacid contributes $\text{-C(=O)-CH=CH-C(=O)-}$.

Assemble one full repeat unit**
Join them as $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-CH=CH-C(=O)-}$ with a dangling bond at the left O and at the right carbonyl C to show continuation of the chain. You must display the ester as $\text{C(=O)-O}$ fully, not just as $\text{COO}$. The trans $\text{C=C}$ remains in the centre.
Final answer: Repeat unit: $\text{-O-CH}_{2}\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-O-C(=O)-CH=CH-C(=O)-}$ with continuation bonds at each end, ester groups shown fully displayed as $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$.

hints: Compare the bonds in the backbone, polar $\text{C-O}$ ester links that water or enzymes can attack versus non-polar $\text{C-C}$ links in a polyalkene.
walkthrough:
Link structure to attack by water**
Think like water trying to break the chain. An ester $\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ has strongly polar $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-O}$ bonds with a partial positive carbon that is easily attacked by water or by enzymes, splitting the chain back to acid plus alcohol. A polyalkene is just a long chain of non-polar $\text{C-C}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bonds with no site for nucleophilic attack, so hydrolysis is impossible and microbes cannot readily break it down.
Final answer: Polyesters contain polar ester linkages that can be broken by hydrolysis, whereas polyalkenes contain only non-polar $\text{C-C}$ bonds that cannot be hydrolysed.

hints: Recognise P as $\text{HO}_{2}\text{C-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ with two identical chiral centres, so expect a pair of enantiomers plus one meso form, three stereoisomers in total.

Keep the backbone $\text{HO}_{2}\text{C-C-C-CO}_{2}\text{H}$ fixed and only swap wedge and dash positions of $\text{OH}$ and $\text{H}$ on the two central carbons to generate the mirror image and the meso form.
walkthrough:
See why only three exist**
P is tartaric acid, $\text{HO}_{2}\text{C-CH(OH)-CH(OH)-CO}_{2}\text{H}$. Each central carbon is bonded to $\text{HO}_{2}\text{C}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{H}$ and the other $\text{CH(OH)CO}_{2}\text{H}$, so both carbons are chiral and identical. Normally that would give four combinations, but the $\text{(R,S)}$ and $\text{(S,R)}$ arrangements are identical by symmetry, the meso form.

Draw the missing two**
The structure already drawn is one optically active form, for example both $\text{OH}$ groups arranged to give $\text{(R,R)}$. Its enantiomer is the exact mirror image, swap every solid wedge to a hashed wedge and vice versa on both centres to give $\text{(S,S)}$. The third is the meso diastereomer, put one $\text{OH}$ on a wedge and the other $\text{OH}$ on a dash so the molecule has opposite configurations at the two centres and is achiral.

Final answer: One box: meso form with one $\text{OH}$ on wedge and the other $\text{OH}$ on dash (opposite faces, e.g. $\text{(2R,3S)}$), giving an internal plane of symmetry. Other box: the mirror image enantiomer of the given structure with both wedges and dashes reversed.

hints: Start with the shape relationship between fumarate and the active site of fumarase, what does complementary mean for binding.
Think about what happens immediately after binding, what named complex is formed and how the enzyme holds the substrate.
Finish the cycle by considering what leaves the enzyme and what happens to the enzyme itself, ready for the next turnover.
walkthrough:
Show specific recognition**
Draw the enzyme as a large shape with a small hollow labelled active site, and the fumarate ion as a smaller shape that exactly fits that hollow. The key idea is complementarity in shape and charge, only fumarate plus water fit fumarase, which is why enzymes are specific.

Form the enzyme-substrate complex**
Draw or describe the substrate moving into the active site and being held by weak interactions such as hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions. This is the ES complex. Binding strains bonds and brings reactants together in the correct orientation, lowering the activation energy.

Release products and regenerate enzyme**
Show the reaction occurring in the active site to give malate, then malate leaving the active site. Emphasise the enzyme itself is unchanged and free to catalyse another reaction. Your diagram must label enzyme, active site, substrate, ES complex, enzyme plus products.

Final answer: Substrate shape is complementary to the active site; substrate binds/fits into the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released leaving the enzyme unchanged. Labelled diagram showing enzyme with active site, substrate, ES complex, enzyme plus products.
